intro:
These exercises take the chapter's three-stage mental model and make it concrete. Inference is pre-processing, a session run, and post-processing; the runtime owns only the middle box, and everything that crosses the boundaries on either side is ordinary Rust you write and are responsible for. The work here is about owning those boundaries correctly: building a tensor whose shape and dtype match the graph's declared contract, slicing a batch without copying, turning raw logits into a calibrated decision, and diagnosing the mismatches that the runtime cannot fix for you.

The code listings are deliberately a pure-Rust forward pass over one dense layer rather than a live ONNX Runtime session, because the arithmetic is identical to what a one-layer Gemm graph performs. That lets you reason about the exact numbers by hand and keep your attention on the parts that are genuinely yours: shapes, dtypes, label maps, session lifecycle, and the runtime-and-provider decision that your build and deploy story can actually accept.

exerciseSolutions.title: Name what the session owns and what you own
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The pipeline has three stages in order. First, pre-processing: raw input (a feature vector, an image, a row of records) is turned into an input tensor with a specific shape and dtype. The data that crosses into the next stage is a tensor that must match the graph's named input declaration. Second, the session run: the runtime takes that input tensor and produces output tensors, which for a classifier are the logits. The data crossing this boundary is one or more output tensors. Third, post-processing: those output tensors become a domain decision, for example a class index plus a confidence, by code such as argmax or softmax. The data crossing out is a decision your application can act on.

The runtime owns exactly one stage: the middle session run. It executes the frozen graph of arithmetic correctly given a conforming input. The two ends, pre-processing and post-processing, are ordinary Rust that you write and own. The chapter's phrasing is that the session owns the math; you own the contract that feeds and reads it.

This is why the chapter says the runtime makes the math correct but does nothing to make shapes, dtypes, and label maps correct. The runtime will faithfully multiply and add whatever conforming buffer you hand it, but it has no knowledge of whether you built the tensor in the right shape, used the right dtype, or mapped output index 1 to the right human label. Those are decisions outside the graph, so they stay your responsibility and they are where inference quietly goes wrong.

Mapping the chapter's listings onto this pipeline: forward, the matmul-against-weights plus bias add, is the session's arithmetic. It is exactly what a single Gemm operator would compute inside the graph, so it stands in for the middle box. argmax is caller-owned post-processing on the far end of the pipeline. It takes the output logits and produces the class decision, and the runtime never does it for you.
criteria: Names pre-processing (build the input tensor), the session run (tensor to output tensors), and post-processing (output tensors to a domain decision) in that order.
States that the runtime owns only the middle box and that both ends are caller-owned Rust code.
Maps forward to the session's Gemm arithmetic and argmax to caller-owned post-processing.
Explains that shape, dtype, and label-map correctness is the caller's responsibility, not the runtime's.

exerciseSolutions.title: Trace one input through the dense layer and argmax
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The dense layer computes logits[o] = bias[o] + sum_c weights[o][c] * input[c] for each output class o, which is one dot product of the input vector with weight row o, plus that row's bias. With input [0.5, -1.0, 2.0, 0.25] and the chapter's WEIGHTS and BIAS, work each row.

Class 0: 0.1 + (0.2 * 0.5) + (0.8 * -1.0) + (-0.5 * 2.0) + (0.1 * 0.25) = 0.1 + 0.10 - 0.80 - 1.00 + 0.025 = -1.5750.

Class 1: -0.2 + (-0.3 * 0.5) + (0.5 * -1.0) + (0.9 * 2.0) + (0.4 * 0.25) = -0.2 - 0.15 - 0.50 + 1.80 + 0.10 = 1.0500.

Class 2: 0.05 + (0.6 * 0.5) + (-0.2 * -1.0) + (0.3 * 2.0) + (-0.7 * 0.25) = 0.05 + 0.30 + 0.20 + 0.60 - 0.175 = 0.9750.

So logits are approximately [-1.5750, 1.0500, 0.9750]. argmax compares the raw logits and never normalizes, so the largest raw value wins: index 1 at 1.0500 beats index 2 at 0.9750 and index 0 at -1.5750. argmax returns 1, and the printed score is logits[1], approximately 1.0500.

This is exactly what a one-layer ONNX model would produce. The matmul-plus-bias is the Gemm operator the runtime runs inside the graph; argmax is caller-owned post-processing that the runtime does not perform. Note that argmax operates on raw logits, so it gives the same answer whether or not you later apply softmax; softmax only changes the reported confidence, not the chosen class.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Hand trace confirmed in code: argmax selects class 1 at score 1.0500.
criteria: Three logits computed as approximately [-1.5750, 1.0500, 0.9750].
argmax selects class 1 because logit[1] is the largest raw value.
Reported score equals logit[1], approximately 1.0500.
Identifies matmul-plus-bias as the runtime's Gemm and argmax as caller-owned post-processing.

exerciseSolutions.title: Add a softmax post-processing stage
exerciseSolutions.solution:
softmax is post-processing you own, exactly like argmax; the runtime does not normalize logits for you. The signature fn softmax(logits: &[f32; OUT]) -> [f32; OUT] borrows the logits immutably and returns a fresh array, so it never mutates its input. That borrow-and-return shape is the calm pattern: the caller keeps owning the logits, and softmax hands back an owned distribution.

The numerically stable form subtracts the maximum logit before exponentiating. exp grows fast, and on f32 a large logit can overflow to infinity, after which the division produces NaN. Subtracting the maximum shifts the largest exponent to exp(0) = 1.0 and makes every other exponent at most 1.0, which cannot overflow. The subtraction does not change the result, because softmax is invariant to adding a constant to all logits: the same factor cancels in numerator and denominator.

The algorithm is three passes: find the maximum, set probs[i] = (logits[i] - max).exp(), then divide every entry by the running total so the vector sums to 1.0. f32 has exp in std, so no external crate is needed.

For the chapter's fixed input the logits are [-1.5750, 1.0500, 0.9750]. After subtracting the max (1.0500) and exponentiating, the distribution is approximately [0.0362, 0.5000, 0.4638], which sums to 1.0000. argmax still picks class 1, and the confidence printed for class 1 is approximately 0.5000. Note that class 1 and class 2 have nearly equal logits, so the model is barely more than a coin flip between them; that low confidence is information the raw argmax alone would have hidden, which is the practical reason to compute softmax.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Stable softmax borrows logits, returns an owned distribution summing to 1.0.
criteria: softmax borrows the logits and returns a new [f32; OUT] without mutating its input.
Subtracts the maximum logit before exponentiating for numerical stability.
Returned probabilities sum to 1.0 within floating-point rounding.
Confidence printed for class 1 is approximately 0.5000 for the chapter's fixed input.

exerciseSolutions.title: Extend the batch and verify per-row argmax
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The batch is one contiguous row-major Vec<f32>: row 0 occupies indices 0..IN, row 1 occupies IN..2*IN, and so on, exactly how a runtime stores a [rows, features] tensor in memory. Appending a third row means adding IN = 4 more floats to build_batch so the flat buffer holds 12 values. The invariant is that the buffer length stays a multiple of IN; rows = batch.len() / IN then evaluates to 3.

Recovering a row is &batch[r * IN..(r + 1) * IN]. This slice borrows a window into the existing Vec; it allocates nothing and copies nothing. The Vec keeps owning the bytes, and forward_row receives a &[f32] view for the duration of the call. This is the ownership point of the exercise: a borrowed slice gives you per-row access without per-row allocation, which is what makes batched IO cheap.

For a concrete third row [2.0, -1.0, 0.5, 1.0]: class 0 = 0.1 + 0.4 - 0.8 - 0.25 + 0.1 = -0.45; class 1 = -0.2 - 0.6 - 0.5 + 0.45 + 0.4 = -0.45; class 2 = 0.05 + 1.2 + 0.2 + 0.15 - 0.7 = 0.90. argmax selects class 2 with score 0.9000. The loop prints one argmax-and-score line per row, including the new third row.

The reason to batch at all is amortization. Building a session parses, optimizes, and allocates; that cost is paid once. Running it is comparatively cheap. One session run over N rows pays the fixed per-call overhead once and lets the runtime process the whole [N, features] tensor together, which beats N separate single-row runs that each re-pay that overhead.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Third row added; each row is a borrowed stride slice, no per-row allocation.
criteria: Flat Vec<f32> length is a multiple of IN and rows evaluates to 3.
Each row is obtained by slicing the existing buffer with no per-row allocation or copy.
Loop prints one argmax-and-score line per row, including the new third row.
Explains that one session run over N rows amortizes session overhead better than N single-row runs.

exerciseSolutions.title: Diagnose a shape and dtype mismatch
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The graph names each input and fixes its shape and dtype; your tensor must match exactly. The colleague has broken that contract in two different ways, and the two failures are not the same class of bug.

The length-3 input against a fixed [4] input is a shape mismatch. The graph declared a static dimension of 4, so the first Gemm expects a weight matrix of 4 columns multiplied against an input of 4 elements. A length-3 buffer cannot be reshaped to [4] without inventing or dropping a value, so the runtime has enough information to reject it: it checks the supplied tensor's shape against the declared input shape and returns an error from session.run rather than guessing. This is the good case, because it fails loudly at run time.

The f32-versus-i64 buffer is a dtype mismatch, and it is more dangerous. If the runtime validates dtypes it errors the same way as the shape case. But the failure mode the exercise warns about is the path where wrong bytes get reinterpreted: a buffer of i64 values handed in where f32 is expected has the same length in elements but completely different bit patterns, so reading those bytes as f32 produces arbitrary floating-point numbers. The graph then runs end to end and returns confident logits that are nonsense, with no error anywhere. argmax happily picks a class from garbage, and downstream code trusts it.

So the runtime can and should catch the length-3 shape mismatch at run time, while the dtype mismatch is the one that can run and return wrong logits when the bytes are reinterpreted rather than checked. This is exactly why the chapter says the most common inference bug is a shape or dtype mismatch, not a wrong model: the model is correct, the contract feeding it is not.

The smallest fix is to restore the declared contract in the input builder: produce a length-4 buffer of f32 that matches the named graph input, and let the type system carry the dtype. Build the input as [f32; 4] (or a Vec<f32> asserted to length 4) rather than a length-3 vector or an i64 buffer, and assert the length before the run so a future regression fails at the boundary instead of inside the graph.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Input builder pins length to IN and dtype to f32, matching the graph's named input.
criteria: Identifies a length-3 input against a fixed [4] input as a shape mismatch the runtime should reject.
Identifies f32-versus-i64 as a separate dtype failure that can run and produce confident nonsense.
States that the most common inference bug is a shape or dtype mismatch, not a wrong model.
Fix restores the input to a length-4 f32 tensor matching the named graph input.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose ort or tract and a session lifecycle
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The decision is rarely about raw speed on one model; it is about what your build and deploy story can accept.

Constraint A (single binary, cross-compiles cleanly to several targets, no GPU, no native dependencies) points to tract, the pure-Rust path. ort links the native ONNX Runtime, a C++ library, which means a native dependency that must be present and version-matched on every target and that complicates cross-compilation. tract is Rust all the way down, so it builds and cross-compiles like any other crate, links statically into the single binary, and carries no GPU or native runtime requirement. It will not be the fastest possible runtime on a given model, but for this constraint the clean build and deploy story is the deciding factor.

Constraint B (CUDA host, p99 latency matters) points to ort. ort exposes execution providers, so you register them in priority order, for example TensorRT first, then CUDA, then CPU as the final fallback. The runtime assigns each operator to the first provider in that list that supports it and falls back to CPU for anything the accelerator providers cannot run. The CPU provider at the end of the list guarantees the graph always executes even when an operator has no GPU kernel.

In both cases, session construction belongs once at service startup, not per request. Building a session parses the file, optimizes the graph, selects execution providers, and allocates working memory; that is the expensive step. Running the session afterward is comparatively cheap. So construct the session during initialization, store it (behind shared, thread-safe ownership for a multi-threaded server), and reuse it across every request. Rebuilding per request would re-pay the entire load cost on every call and dominate latency.

A concrete tradeoff of the provider ordering beyond raw speed: provider assignment is per operator, so a graph with even one operator the accelerator does not support gets that operator placed on CPU, and the resulting CPU-GPU handoffs copy tensors across the boundary, which can erase the expected latency win and add jitter to p99. Separately, choosing ort with CUDA or TensorRT adds a native dependency and pulls heavy GPU libraries into the deployment image, increasing image size and tying the build to a specific CUDA toolchain. The ordering is a deployment and latency tradeoff, not a free speedup.
criteria: Constraint A selects tract / pure-Rust, justified by clean cross-compilation and no native or GPU dependency.
Constraint B selects ort and registers providers such as CUDA or TensorRT in priority order with CPU fallback.
Places session construction once at startup and reuses it across requests because building a session is the expensive step.
Names a concrete provider tradeoff, such as per-operator placement, CPU fallback handoffs, or added native dependency and image size.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
logits = [-1.5750, 1.0500, 0.9750]
probs = [0.0362, 0.5000, 0.4638]
probs sum = 1.0000
predicted class = 1
confidence = 0.5000
labSolution.explanation:
forward runs the dense layer, computing each logit as bias[o] plus the dot product of the input with weight row o. For the fixed input [0.5, -1.0, 2.0, 0.25] this yields [-1.5750, 1.0500, 0.9750], which is the arithmetic a one-layer ONNX Gemm operator would perform inside the graph.

softmax is the post-processing stage the lab asks you to complete, and it is code you own rather than something the runtime does. It first finds the maximum logit (1.0500) and subtracts it before calling exp, which keeps every exponent at or below exp(0) = 1.0 so nothing overflows on f32; subtracting a constant from all logits does not change the result because the factor cancels in the numerator and denominator. It then divides each exponentiated value by their total so the vector sums to 1.0, giving [0.0362, 0.5000, 0.4638]. argmax operates on the raw logits and selects class 1 because 1.0500 is the largest, and the confidence printed is probs[1], which is 0.5000.

The near-tie between class 1 and class 2 in the logits is exactly why softmax is useful: argmax alone reports class 1 with no sense of how marginal that choice is, while the 0.5000 confidence shows the model is barely past a coin flip. The program compiles with only the standard library because exp is a method on f32, so it prints the expected output with no external crate.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is ONNX described as a contract, and what does standardizing operators and tensor declarations let a producer and consumer do independently?
reviewAnswers.answer: ONNX is a contract because the exported file fixes the graph's operators and its named input and output tensor declarations in a standardized form that any conforming runtime understands. A producer can train in any framework (PyTorch, TensorFlow, scikit-learn) and export to ONNX without knowing or caring which runtime will load it. A consumer can load that one file into whichever runtime fits its deployment, and because the operators and tensor declarations are standardized, the same graph runs unchanged. The two sides are decoupled: the training framework and the serving runtime can be chosen and changed independently as long as both honor the file's contract.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is building a session the expensive step, and what operational habit does that justify in a request-serving service?
reviewAnswers.answer: Building a session is expensive because it parses the model file, optimizes the graph, selects and initializes execution providers, and allocates working memory; that is a substantial amount of one-time work. Running the session afterward is comparatively cheap, mostly the arithmetic over your input. The operational habit this justifies is build once, run many: construct the session a single time at service startup and reuse it across every request, behind thread-safe shared ownership for a multi-threaded server. Rebuilding the session per request would re-pay the entire load cost on every call and would dominate request latency.

reviewAnswers.question: What role does ndarray play for ONNX inference in Rust, and what does a tensor consist of beyond its raw buffer?
reviewAnswers.answer: ndarray plays the role NumPy plays in Python: it owns the flat data buffer and tracks the shape so the runtime can interpret the bytes correctly, which is the usual way to build the input and read the output tensors in Rust. A tensor is more than its raw buffer; it is a flat buffer plus a shape and a dtype. The shape tells the runtime how to index the buffer as a multidimensional array, and the dtype tells it how to interpret each element's bytes. The graph names each input and output and fixes its shape and dtype, so the tensor you build with ndarray must match that declaration exactly.

reviewAnswers.question: What does an execution provider decide, and why is registering providers in priority order a deployment and latency tradeoff rather than a free speedup?
reviewAnswers.answer: An execution provider decides where the operators actually run, for example on CPU, CUDA, or TensorRT. With ort you register providers in priority order, and the runtime assigns each operator to the first provider in that list that supports it, falling back to CPU for the rest. This is a tradeoff rather than a free speedup because placement is per operator: a graph with even one operator the accelerator does not support gets that operator on CPU, and the CPU-GPU handoffs copy tensors across the boundary, which can erase the expected win and add latency jitter. Choosing a GPU provider also adds a native dependency, pulls heavy libraries into the image, and ties the build to a specific toolchain, all of which are deployment costs beyond raw speed.

reviewAnswers.question: When a tensor borrows a Vec for a session run, what does the borrow checker enforce, and what is the calm pattern for owning inputs and outputs around the run?
reviewAnswers.answer: Tensors borrow their backing buffers, so the borrow checker enforces that a tensor viewing a Vec cannot outlive that buffer; the Vec must stay alive and unmoved for as long as the tensor references it during the run. This does real work here by preventing the session from reading freed or relocated memory. The calm pattern is to build owned inputs, hand the session a tensor that borrows them just for the run, and then copy or map the output tensors into owned domain types before the borrows end. That way ownership is clear on both ends: you own the input Vec and the output decision, and the borrowed tensor view exists only for the duration of the session call.
